China just had its best earnings season in years:

Profits at Chinese companies listed in mainland China surged +25.7% YoY in Q2 2026, the highest growth rate since Q2 2021.

This also marks the 2nd consecutive quarter of positive earnings growth following a double-digit decline in Q4 2025.

The surge was driven by AI-linked companies, with earnings up +42% on Shenzhen’s growth-focused ChiNext market and +370% on Shanghai’s technology-focused STAR Market, significantly outpacing the broader market.

Despite this outstanding performance, the CSI 300 Index has fallen -9% so far this quarter, while the tech-heavy STAR 50 Index has dropped -29%.

China is experiencing a historic earnings boom due to AI.

BREAKING: The 4-week average of US new home listings rose +2.1% in the week ending August 30th, to 383,795, its highest since August 2022.

This exceeds this year’s previous peak of 383,712, set in April.

The increase was led by San Jose, Boston, and Nashville, where listings surged +29.4%, +26.1%, and +21.5%, respectively.

At the same time, the total number of homes for sale rose +0.4% to 1,511,313.

Meanwhile, pending home sales declined -0.1% over the same period to 308,282, the lowest since February, suggesting demand is failing to keep up with rising supply.

This comes as the median sale price rose +2.2% YoY to $398,632, while the average 30Y mortgage rate stood at 6.66%, near its highest over the last 12 months.

Housing market affordability is at record lows.

The bull market is gaining momentum:

The 200-day moving average of the S&P 500 has now risen for 329 consecutive trading sessions, the 4th-strongest streak over the last 10 years.

This follows a previous 460-session run that briefly ended in April 2025 following "Liberation Day," bringing the combined streak to ~800 sessions, which would be the 3rd-longest since 1990.

For perspective, the longest such stretch lasted 1,448 days during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.

Historically, when the 200-day moving average was rising, the S&P 500 returned +8.5% per year on average since 1999.

By comparison, when the 200-day moving average was falling, the S&P 500 returned just +0.1% per year on average.

History suggests the bullish trend is far from over.

The current decline in US bonds is unprecedented:

15+ year Treasuries have returned -2% per year on average over the last 10 years, their worst performance in history.

This is also only the 2nd period in data going back to 1936 where Treasuries have posted negative 10-year annualized returns.

By comparison, US stocks have returned +15% per year on average, while commodities have returned +11% per year on average over the same timeframe.

To put this into perspective, before the 2020 pandemic, Treasuries gained +9% per year on average over a 10-year period.

Since the start of 2020, the popular bond-tracking ETF $TLT has dropped -26%, with its biggest drawdown at -34%.

The bond market is no longer the safe haven it once was.

Last week, SpaceX and Governor Jeff Landry announced Starbase Louisiana, a $100 billion commitment to build one of the largest infrastructure projects in history on roughly 125,000 acres at Pecan Island in Vermilion Parish.

The greenfield investment includes five complexes, each with two Starship towers, with ten pads at the outset, and eventually more than a dozen towers supporting ~30 flights per day. The land will include not only a launch site, but also onsite propellant production, power generation, deep-water shipping, vehicle processing, employee housing, and likely an airport.

Construction will begin in 2027, with first launches no earlier than 2029.

Gwynne Shotwell was clear about the motivation: the company's existing infrastructure—two pads at Starbase in Texas and three soon-to-be in Florida—cannot support the ambitious plans for Starship’s flight cadence.

For perspective on the scope of the project, Brazil’s 14 gigawatt (GW) Itaipu hydropower plant, the closest completed contemporary analog, cost ~$90 billion in today’s dollars, and California’s much delayed and uncompleted high-speed rail project is projected to cost ~$125 billion.

@wintonARK details more in our recent newsletter ⬇️

Copper just hit an all-time high, $14,533 a ton. Read the reason before you call it inflation.

This record was manufactured by a tariff threat. Traders front-running possible US copper levies shipped hundreds of thousands of tons into American warehouses to capture the Comex premium, drained the LME's global stockpiles to critical lows, and forced a squeeze. Spot now trades above futures, a backwardation that signals scarcity, in a market where physical demand is soft.

That is the whole lesson on tariffs. A tariff is a one-time price shock and a distortion in relative prices, never a source of sustained inflation: one metal, one border, one policy. When Commerce finally rules, the arbitrage closes, the hoarded US metal releases, and the squeeze unwinds. Real inflation comes from the printing press. This came from the customs house.

$CPER

The great EV transition just threw itself into reverse.

After hundreds of billions in stranded capital chasing a mostly-electric market by the 2030s, the auto industry's new fix for range anxiety is a gas engine. Hyundai, Ford and Jeep-maker Stellantis are rolling out extended-range EVs: a battery car with a gas generator bolted on to recharge it.

The Ram 1500 REV promises up to 690 miles, more than double a typical US EV. Ford is resurrecting the electric F-150 Lightning it killed last December, this time with a gas engine. Hyundai's Santa Fe version targets 600 miles in 2027.

Here is the lesson for every policy-driven boom. EV sales sank the moment the $7,500 subsidy went away. Mandates and incentives can pull an industry's capex forward by years, but when the check stops, real demand reasserts itself and the stranded assets land on shareholders. The same script is being written right now in AI and solar.

The AI trade has a weather problem the market refuses to price.

Nearly 40% of US data-center capacity sits in tornado-prone zones. The newest builds are the most exposed of all: 43% of capacity under construction, versus 37% already operating. They are building deeper into the storm.

These are single assets worth $20 billion to $50 billion each, with zero claims history. Swiss Re pegs the insurance market for them at $30 billion a year by 2030, and even then, no single insurer can absorb the risk alone.

So the hyperscalers self-insure the tail. The same megacaps holding up the S&P 500 are carrying catastrophe risk on their own balance sheets. One tornado in data-center alley sets off multiple billion-dollar claims at once. AI concentration risk now has a weather map, and it runs through Texas and Virginia.

Wall Street wants you to believe pensions are making a comeback. Look at the actual chart.

In 1989, pensions and 401(k)s each covered about 29% of private-sector workers. Today pensions cover 7%. 401(k)-type plans cover 52%.

Cash-balance employers went from 23,000 to 26,000 in three years, and most of those new pensions still hand the market risk back to you.

Here is what the chart actually says. Over 35 years, companies moved retirement off their balance sheet and onto yours, and they are not moving it back. Your retirement is your job. Fund it like no one is coming to rescue it, because for 93% of private workers, no one is.
